nodes.body: It was the last week of October. The big Bramley apple tree at the top of the hill was covered in white flowers. Every other tree on the slope was bare, their black branches against a grey sky. But the old tree had bloomed like it was May. Jonah stood in the wet grass and stared. The blossom stared back, silent and strange. Its early, wrong bloom was the only one around.

choices.label: Go and tell Ada what you have seen.

nodes.body: Ada was in the shed writing the day up in a ruled notebook, the way she had every evening since before Jonah was born. The paraffin heater ticked in the corner and the air smelled of old paper and cold earth. Jonah told her about the blossom, and she did not look up from the page. She did not look surprised either, which was worse than if she had. Her pen kept moving, a faint scratch in the quiet. "I know," she said at last, and the words landed like a stone in still water. Three paths opened in Jonah's mind, each pulling a different direction, and none of them felt like the obviously right one.

choices.label: Ask whether the notebooks have seen this before.
Go and stand by the hives instead.
Go down and read the notice on the gate.

nodes.body: Ada turned back through decades of her own handwriting. Page after page, October after October, the dates ran backwards under her thumb. She looked at blossom dates, frost dates, and picking dates. Not one of them was like this one. The shed smelled of old apples and paraffin. The silence grew. Jonah watched her search and saw a loose sheet of paper tucked inside the back of the 1952 book. It was in a different hand. It was a note from Ada's own mother, listing every strange thing the orchard had ever done. Ada had forgotten it was there. She pressed it flat on the bench and read it twice. Then she nodded slowly.

choices.label: Begin with what the record already holds.

nodes.body: The hives along the south fence were loud at four on a cold afternoon. The humming should not have been there in October. The bees were out and working, tricked by the warmth the blossom had promised. Their sound was wrong in the thin autumn light. Later, Mrs. Cassar told Jonah that bees did not do this. Not in the last week before the frosts. She had not seen anything like it in thirty years of keeping bees.

choices.label: Begin with what the bees are doing.

nodes.body: A covered notice had appeared on the orchard gate since morning. It was tied at all four corners by someone who meant it to stay. It was an early science survey summary, typed and official. It looked out of place against the old wood and the wet weeds. Jonah read it through twice. The second time the words felt heavier. He took out his phone and took a photo. The bare trees were behind it. He only thought he wanted a record. Later that would turn out to be the only picture anyone had of the notice in place.

choices.label: Begin with the notice itself.

nodes.body: Six shelves of notebooks filled the far wall of the shed. They ran from 1911 to this evening. Over the years, nine different people had written in them. There was no index, no list, no key. Everything anyone knew about this hill was in there. Weather, blossom, picking weights, wasp years, frost years, the price of ladders. Jonah stood in front of the shelves. He felt the weight of a hundred and fourteen years pressing back. The notebooks were an argument waiting to be made. But making it meant choosing where to start.

choices.label: Find out who wrote the survey.
Find out what the survey left out.
Ask what a hundred years of weather notes are worth.

nodes.body: The survey was signed at the bottom of the last page: D. Faulks, dated in August. Jonah wrote the name down in the back of his exercise book and stared at it. A name was a starting point. It felt like a loose thread you could pull, and Jonah had a feeling that pulling it would unravel something. He closed the notebook and went to find Ada.

choices.label: Find out who wrote the survey.

nodes.body: Mrs. Cassar kept her own hive records in a stack of spiral notebooks in her kitchen. Her counts did not match Jonah's by a wide margin. She had counted two hundred and forty bees searching for food on the warm side of the hives that afternoon. Jonah had counted fewer than half that. They sat at her table and compared their figures. The gap between them did not close. One of them had been counting the wrong thing all autumn. Neither could say which.

choices.label: Copy the sentence out and take it home.
Stay in the shed until the light goes.
Walk the rows and count the trees.

nodes.body: The notice was an early science survey summary. It was printed on both sides and dated in August. Jonah read it standing at the gate with cold fingers. The sentence that mattered was eleven words long: the site is of no particular scientific interest. Eleven words dismissed a hundred and fourteen years of records. Nine hands, six shelves, and a tree flowering in the wrong month. Jonah read the sentence again. He felt something tighten in his chest.

choices.label: Ask Ada who else wrote in these.
Photograph the notice before anything happens to it.
Find out who wrote the survey.

nodes.body: The survey was signed D. Faulks and dated in August. In August, a century-old orchard looks like nothing much: long grass and shade. Anyone walking through in high summer would see unpruned branches, weeds, and a pond thick with duckweed. No reason to stop. The signature sat at the bottom of the page, neat and small, as if the name itself was trying not to be seen. Jonah stared at it. He thought about what a person sees when they are not looking for anything in particular.

choices.label: Find out how a survey gets challenged.
Find out what Faulks actually looked at.
Find somebody who reads old records for a living.

nodes.body: Every survey has a method section. It's a paragraph that tells you how the work was done. This one listed four site visits over eleven days. All of them were dry, and none of them lasted longer than an hour. Jonah read the times and added them up in his head. Four hours, spread across a fortnight in August. On that basis, someone had written eleven words. Those words could erase a hundred and fourteen years. The numbers felt like a door closing.

choices.label: Find somebody who studies the ground itself.
Find out what the developer actually wants.
Ask Tobe to help with the numbers.

nodes.body: Ada said the notebooks were only the weather, nothing more. She said weather by itself proved nothing. Jonah said the weather was the whole argument. A tree that flowered in October was weather you could see. They stood in the shed with the heater ticking. The argument hung between them, unprovable. Ada had written the day up every evening for sixty years. She did not believe the notebooks could change anything. Jonah could not show her that she was wrong. Not standing there with the light going.

choices.label: Let the six weeks run out.
Find out how a survey gets challenged.
Find out what Faulks actually looked at.

nodes.body: Jonah copied the eleven words into the back of an exercise book. He sat at the kitchen table with a pencil that needed sharpening. The sentence looked smaller in his own handwriting. It also looked worse. It sat on the page like a thing decided somewhere else. It had been delivered here without warning. He closed the book and put it in his pocket. The words went with him.

choices.label: Find somebody who reads old records for a living.

nodes.body: The shed had one light bulb on a wire, swinging a little in the draft from the door. The oldest notebooks sat on the top shelf above it, where the light did not reach. Their spines had all faded to the same grey. Jonah stood on a crate and ran a finger along them, feeling the years in the dark. He thought about all the evenings people had written up in worse light than this.

choices.label: Find somebody who studies the ground itself.

nodes.body: Jonah walked the rows counting trees, touching each trunk to keep the number steady. He got to three hundred and ninety-one somewhere near the pond. Then a moorhen clattered out of the reeds and the number went clean out of his head. He started again from the top of the hill. This time the count came out differently, and he understood that counting was not as simple as it sounded.

choices.label: Find out what the developer actually wants.

nodes.body: Nine different hands had written in the notebooks over the years, Ada told him. She could name eight of them without thinking. The ninth was a small neat pencil that appeared in 1939 and stopped in 1943 without a word of why. Four years of careful entries and then nothing. Ada said she had never been able to work out who that writer was or why they stopped.

choices.label: Ask Tobe to help with the numbers.

nodes.body: Jonah photographed the notice with the bare trees behind it. The zip-ties looked sharp against the grey sky. Then he went home and did not look at the picture again for weeks. Much later, when the notice had been taken down and nobody could say exactly what it had said or when it had appeared, that photograph turned out to be the only one anyone had of it in place.

choices.label: Let the six weeks run out.

nodes.body: Objections closed in six weeks. The form Jonah downloaded from the council website asked for proof of scientific interest. The phrase sat in bold type halfway down the first page. It was the exact same phrase the survey had used to say there was none. Someone had written the form and someone else had written the survey. The two documents had been designed to fit together like a lock and a key. Jonah read the form three times. Each time the same sentence stared back at him, waiting to be answered.

choices.label: Work out how many pages there actually are.
Work out which years matter most.
Work out how to read the difficult hands.

nodes.body: The four survey visits were logged to the half hour: nine-fifteen to ten, two-thirty to three-fifteen, and so on. Jonah added them up on a scrap of paper. They came to just under four hours. Not one visit had lasted long enough to walk the whole orchard. They had no time to open a hive or count the species in the pond. Four hours in August. On that basis, someone had written a sentence. That sentence could bring eighty-two houses and a spine road straight through the row where the big Bramley stood.

choices.label: Work out who is allowed to touch them.
Work out where to do the work.
Work out how to prove you copied it right.

nodes.body: The city archive kept a Tuesday desk. The archivist there had seen a great many shoeboxes brought in by people who believed they were holding something important. She was not impressed by any of them yet. Her name was Mrs Okonkwo and she listened to Jonah's story with her hands folded on the desk. When he finished she said only, "Show me what you have." It was not a dismissal and it was not a boost. It was somehow exactly the right thing to say.

choices.label: Open the 1911 volume first.
Set the laptop up on the shed bench.
Take the folding table down to the orchard.

nodes.body: The university website listed a Dr Ines Abara under Long Term Monitoring. That phrase turned out to mean exactly what the six shelves were. Her research page showed a photo of a woman in her forties standing by a weather station in a field. Her work listed papers on thirty-year butterfly counts and sixty-year soil heat records. Jonah read the page twice. For the first time since the blossom, he felt that someone might already understand what they had.

choices.label: Ask Ada to read the hard pages aloud.
Photograph one page as a test.
Make a list of every year that is missing.

nodes.body: The plan was eighty-two homes and a spine road, printed on a glossy brochure the developer had left in the village hall. The road ran in a straight line from the new roundabout to the edge of the parish. The straight line went directly along the row the big Bramley stood in. Jonah traced the route with his finger. He saw that the tree was not just in the way of the road. It was exactly where the road wanted to be. Someone had drawn a line on a map without knowing what was on the ground, or without caring.

choices.label: Stop and eat something.
Try to do all of it at once.
Work out how many pages there actually are.

nodes.body: Tobe ran the school weather club, owned a laptop that actually worked, and thought a hundred years of bloom dates was the finest thing he had ever been offered. He sat in the shed with a notebook on his knee and listened while Jonah explained. By the end of it he was grinning. "This is better than the rainfall project," he said. "This is better than everything." He opened the laptop and flexed his fingers above the keyboard like someone about to play a difficult piece of music.

choices.label: Work out which years matter most.
Work out how to read the difficult hands.
Work out who is allowed to touch them.

nodes.body: The notebooks went back on the shelf. The objection window closed without Jonah in it. The six weeks passed in ordinary days: school and weather and evenings in the shed. By the time anyone thought to ask what had happened, the deadline was already behind them. What Jonah was left with was a photo of a notice on a gate, the eleven words still in the back of an exercise book, and a clear idea of what he had not done. The Bramley stood at the top of the hill in the rain. Its blossom was long since blown away. The gate stayed shut.

Tobe counted sample pages and multiplied on the back of an envelope. The answer came out somewhere near forty thousand daily lines. He read the number aloud and the kitchen went quiet. Forty thousand lines of weather, blossom, frost, wasps, picking weights, and the price of things. Ada put her cup down and did not pick it up again. The number sat in the middle of the table like an object that had weight. Nobody wanted to be the first to say what they were all thinking. Forty thousand lines was too many, and the six weeks were too short.

choices.label: Take the four lines a year approach.
Take the whole record but only for the Bramleys.
Take the hive counts as well.

nodes.body: Tobe pointed out that they didn't have to type everything. The argument didn't need every detail. It needed bloom dates and frost dates, which was four lines a year. Four lines times a hundred and fourteen years came to four hundred and fifty-six numbers. That was a task you could hold in your head, not forty thousand lines, and it was still a century of proof. Ada nodded slowly, the way she did when something settled into place. Jonah felt the impossible weight of the job lift a little.

choices.label: Ask the archive to hold the originals.
Ask Dr Abara what would count as evidence.
Ask Tobe to build the chart.

nodes.body: The 1920s handwriting leaned so far to the right that a three and a five looked almost the same. The ink had faded to a pale brown that caught the light in a new way on every page. Getting one digit wrong by two would put a bloom date in the wrong week. A wrong week was all someone like Faulks needed to throw out the whole set. Jonah held the page up to the bulb and squinted. The number refused to become clear. The past could be read, but only just, and only if you were careful.

choices.label: Ask the school if the class can help.
Ask what happens if you are wrong.
Ask Ada what she wants out of this.

nodes.body: Ada had never let a notebook leave the shed, not once in sixty years. The archive would not take anything it could not see and check in person. Both sides made sense, and both meant the notebooks stayed right where they were. On the six shelves, with the single bulb, the paraffin heater, and the draft under the door. Jonah stood in the middle of the shed, feeling two walls of the argument pushing in from both sides. Neither one would move.

choices.label: Hand the whole thing to the archive and step back.
Send the chart out before it is checked.

nodes.body: Jonah remembered the photo on his phone, the notice zip-tied to the gate with the bare trees behind it. He pulled it up on the screen. The eleven words were sharp and clear, and the date stamp proved exactly when the notice had appeared. Tobe looked at it. "That's evidence they didn't put it up until October," he said. The picture changed the argument. It was not just a record now, but proof that the survey had been posted late. This cut the objection window shorter than it should have been. Tobe added the photo to the file.

choices.label: Take the four lines a year approach.

nodes.body: The shed was cold and had one socket. It was fixed to a board nailed to the wall in the 1970s. The kitchen had a table, but Ada did not want the books in the house. Someone might spill tea on them or put them away without knowing the right order. The school hall was free on Thursdays. It had heating, tables, and a plug socket for every laptop. The caretaker said yes before Jonah had even finished asking.

choices.label: Take the whole record but only for the Bramleys.
Take the hive counts as well.
Ask the archive to hold the originals.

nodes.body: A number typed from a page was just a claim about a page, Tobe said. And claims were not evidence. The fix was boring. Photograph every page you typed, so anyone who doubted a number could check the original. "It doubles the work," Tobe said, "but it makes the work solid." Jonah looked at the six shelves and thought about the task being twice as big. Then he nodded, because solid was exactly what they needed.

choices.label: Ask Dr Abara what would count as evidence.
Ask Tobe to build the chart.
Ask the school if the class can help.

nodes.body: The first volume opened with a crack. The binding creaked as Jonah laid it flat on the archive desk. The opening page was covered in tight, neat writing. It began with the price of ladders in March 1911. Then, with no big title, it gave the first bloom date. April the fourteenth. The ink had barely faded. Under it was a note about a late frost that had blackened the blossom on the lower row. Over a century of watching had started with ladders and frost, just the way it kept going.

choices.label: Ask what happens if you are wrong.

nodes.body: The laptop sat on the shed bench between a sack of wax and a jar of screws. The extension lead ran out under the door and across the grass to the house. It was not a lasting fix, Ada said. The first rain would find the connection and trip the fuse. But it worked for now. The screen glowed blue in the dim shed, and Jonah typed the first line of the first year. Ada read it aloud over his shoulder.

choices.label: Ask Ada what she wants out of this.

nodes.body: The folding table went down the hill on the wheelbarrow. It bumped over roots and molehills and came to rest on level ground by the pond. It was the only flat spot in the whole orchard. The light was good there, coming through the bare branches of the willows. Jonah set up the laptop and the first notebook. He worked to the sound of water and the odd splash of a frog. The work felt different outdoors. It felt less like a fight and more like something that was always meant to happen here.

choices.label: Hand the whole thing to the archive and step back.

nodes.body: Ada read the 1920s pages out loud while Jonah typed. She read them the way a person reads things they half remember. Her voice slowed on certain dates. The ones where a late frost caught the blossom or a wet summer brought the wasps. Jonah could hear in the pauses that she was not just reading. She was remembering, or remembering being told, or maybe both. The past came through her voice into the laptop. The numbers on the screen felt warmer than numbers usually did.

choices.label: Send the chart out before it is checked.

nodes.body: The first photo came out with Jonah's own shadow across the numbers. The dark shape wiped out the very figures he was trying to save. He learned fast to stand to the side of the light. He held the phone at an angle that caught the ink without catching himself. The second photo was better. The third was almost perfect. By the end of the afternoon, he had a system.

choices.label: Take the four lines a year approach.

nodes.body: There was no 1917 volume and no 1918 volume. There was no note anywhere saying where they had gone. The gap on the shelf was the width of two fingers. The dust in it was the same grey as the dust on either side. That meant the books had been missing for a very long time. Jonah put his fingers into the gap and felt the rough wood. The loss of those two years felt like a question that no one alive could answer.

choices.label: Take the whole record but only for the Bramleys.

nodes.body: Jonah ate toast standing up at nine at night with cold hands. The laptop was still glowing on the shed bench behind him. Ada poured tea and said this was what the work was, mostly, and always had been: late nights and cold fingers and the feeling that you had not done enough. She said it without complaint, as a fact. Jonah understood that she was not warning him off but welcoming him in.

choices.label: Take the hive counts as well.

nodes.body: Jonah started at 1911, meaning to type everything: every line, every note, every observation. By the fourth evening, the pages blurred in front of his eyes and the numbers stopped meaning anything. The six weeks were shorter than they had been, and the task was larger than it had seemed. The laptop sat on the bench with only twelve years completed. The remaining century pressed down like a weight. The deadline was no longer a distant thing but something he could feel in his chest when he breathed. He had tried to do all of it at once, and all of it had been too much.

First bloom, full bloom, last frost, first picking: those were the four dates that mattered. They told the story of the orchard year by year. A century of four dates was four hundred and fifty-six numbers instead of forty thousand. Four hundred and fifty-six was a number you could hold in your head. It was a task that could be finished before the deadline. Tobe set up the spreadsheet with four columns and a hundred and fourteen rows. The empty cells looked almost manageable, like a field waiting to be planted.

choices.label: Set up a check by two people.
Set up a rule for unreadable figures.
Bring Mrs Cassar in properly.

nodes.body: One row of trees all the way back, the Bramleys only, was fewer numbers. It was also a much easier argument to explain out loud to somebody who was in a hurry. You could point at the row and say, these trees, this record, this century. The person listening could see the trees with their own eyes. The rest of the orchard would have to speak for itself later. But for now the Bramleys were the case, and the case was simple enough to fit in a single sentence.

choices.label: Bring Dr Abara up the hill.
Bring the school class in.
Go and find the missing volumes.

nodes.body: Mrs Cassar had thirty years of her own hive records and was willing to share them. She wanted it understood that her early counts were done differently. She had changed her method in 2005 and again in 2014. The numbers from before and after those years were not quite the same thing. "I'm not pretending otherwise," she said. The way she said it made clear that pretending otherwise was the thing she would not do, under any circumstances, for anyone.

choices.label: Go and see Priya Raval at the council.
Print the first proper chart.
Walk the frost pocket at dawn.

nodes.body: The archivist, Mrs Okonkwo, offered a shelf in a room with a stable temperature. She offered a receipt on proper letterhead, and the right for Ada to see the notebooks any weekday she liked. The room was on the first floor, and the window faced north so the light would not fade the ink. The door locked with a key that only two people had. It was the best offer anyone was going to make. It meant the notebooks would outlast the argument, whatever the argument decided.

choices.label: Sort the notebooks by hand.
Wait outside the council office.
Carry the carrier bags up the hill.

nodes.body: Dr Abara was careful on the phone, her voice slow and exact. She said a long unbroken local series was truly rare. It was one of the things ecologists hoped to find and almost never did. But it was only evidence, she said, if somebody could show how it had been measured and by whom. Method was everything. Without method, a hundred and fourteen years was just a hundred and fourteen years of someone writing things down. And writing things down was not science.

choices.label: Let Tobe explain the spreadsheet.
Look at the chart for a long time.
Decide the chart is enough on its own.

nodes.body: Tobe put the bloom dates on one axis and the years on the other. The shape that came out was not subtle. The line moved eleven days earlier across the century, a steady creep that anybody could see. The room went quiet while they all looked at it. The quiet said more than words would have. The chart was no longer an argument. It was a fact, made visible, and facts did not need to be defended.

choices.label: Guess at the unreadable figures.
Set up a check by two people.
Set up a rule for unreadable figures.

nodes.body: Thirty pairs of hands could type a century in a fortnight, working in shifts on Thursday afternoons. Thirty pairs of hands could also put a hundred small errors into the spreadsheet. Those errors would be hard to find and impossible to explain later. Jonah sat in the school hall and imagined the room full of people typing, the clatter of keyboards and the focus. He could not decide whether he was picturing a solution or a new problem.

choices.label: Bring Mrs Cassar in properly.
Bring Dr Abara up the hill.
Bring the school class in.

nodes.body: If a single date was out by a fortnight, the whole chart could be questioned. Faulks would only need one error to say the rest could not be trusted. Everybody in the kitchen knew it. The knowledge sat in the middle of the table like a cold cup of tea. Nobody wanted to be the one to say that the whole task might depend on getting every digit exactly right. But the fact was there, unspoken, and it made every keystroke feel heavier than it should.

choices.label: Go and find the missing volumes.
Go and see Priya Raval at the council.
Print the first proper chart.

nodes.body: Ada said she had never once thought of the notebooks as an argument. They were a record, a habit, a way of marking the days. She had written the day up every evening since she was twenty-one because her mother had done it and her grandmother before that. The idea of those careful pages being used to fight a developer made her uneasy in a way she could not quite explain. "I'm not sure I like them becoming a weapon," she said. The word hung in the air of the shed, sharp and strange.

choices.label: Walk the frost pocket at dawn.
Sort the notebooks by hand.
Wait outside the council office.

nodes.body: The notebooks went into the temperature-stable room at the archive. Mrs Okonkwo catalogued them under LOCAL WEATHER: ORCHARD HILL, 1911 TO PRESENT. They were safe forever, the paper protected from damp and sunlight and the slow decay of time. Nobody made the argument. The objection window closed without a single page of the record being used as evidence. The orchard was surveyed again in August by the same method, by the same person, and the result was the same. What Jonah had wanted to say was still there, unspoken, between the lines of every notebook on the shelf.

The chart went round the neighbourhood in an evening. It passed from Tobe's laptop to a phone and then another and then another. It came back the next morning with a correction. It was a date someone's grandfather recalled differently. Jonah could not answer the correction because he had sent the chart before it was checked. After that, people read his next message more slowly and carefully. The trust that had carried the work was harmed in a way he could not fix by saying sorry. The chart was mostly right. But mostly was not enough.

Two people typed every page. They sat at opposite ends of the school hall so they could not see each other's screens. Tobe's laptop compared the two versions and found eleven mismatches in the first hundred pages. A three was a five, a date was flipped, a word was read wrong. Eleven errors in a hundred pages was not many. But it proved the double-typing was needed and the work could not be done by one person alone.

Ask the archive to write a custody note.

nodes.body: Anything truly unclear was marked with a question mark rather than guessed. The marked ones were kept in their own list at the bottom of the spreadsheet for all to see. The list was not long, just nineteen entries out of four hundred and fifty-six. They were a few moments where the ink had failed or a hand had wobbled. By putting the gaps in plain sight, Jonah hid nothing. That openness was a strength of its own.

choices.label: Ask Mrs Cassar to date her method changes.
Ask what Faulks would say to this.
Ask the paper to run something.

nodes.body: Mrs Cassar came to the shed with two carrier bags of hive records. The notebooks were stacked inside with their spines facing the same way. She had one rule, which she gave before she let anyone touch them. Nobody was to pretend her counts were more exact than they were. Her early years were rough guesses, she said. She would not have them dressed up as firm numbers. "I won't be made a liar of after the fact," she said. She said it looking straight at Jonah, and he nodded.

choices.label: Ask the developer for their survey data.
Ask Ada about 1917.
Ask the school to keep the Thursday hall.

nodes.body: Dr Abara walked the rows for two hours in the rain, her coat getting dark with water, and said almost nothing. At the bottom of the hill she stopped by the pond and looked back up the slope. Then she asked if anybody had ever measured the frost pocket. The question hung in the wet air. Jonah saw that he had walked past that dip in the ground a hundred times without ever thinking to put a thermometer in it. Abara nodded slowly, as if the lack of an answer was itself an answer.

choices.label: Take the newspaper offer and stop there.
Say something about Faulks you cannot support.
Say something about Faulks you cannot support.
Ask Raval exactly what she can accept.

nodes.body: Jonah recalled the loose sheet from 1952. It was Ada's mother's list of strange events, and he pulled it from the notebook. The list had a bloom in November 1948 and a frost in June 1953. It proved the orchard had done odd things before. Those things had been written down, checked, and found to be real. Instead of blaming Faulks, Jonah showed Abara the list. He asked if a pattern of odd events was itself proof. Abara read it and said softly, "Yes. That is exactly what it is." The blame faded before it was spoken, and the argument grew stronger.

nodes.body: The Thursday hall filled with thirty people typing. The noise was huge and strange in a room that usually held assemblies and lunch lines. Keyboards clattered. The young ones asked questions and the older ones peered at the faded pages. By four in the afternoon the 1930s were done. Mrs Cassar brought tea in a flask and Ada walked between the tables, looking at the screens. The work that had seemed too big in the shed became simple and shared in a room full of people.

choices.label: Ask Abara to write about the frost pocket.
Ask the archive to write a custody note.
Ask Mrs Cassar to date her method changes.

nodes.body: Two volumes were missing from the shelf, 1917 and 1918. Somebody must have taken them somewhere. The shed was not the only building on this hill. There was the old packing shed down by the road. There was the stone bothy that had been a home during the war. And there was the loft above the garage where Ada's father had kept his tools. Somewhere in one of those spaces, or somewhere else at all, two years of weather and blossom might still be waiting to be found.

choices.label: Ask what Faulks would say to this.
Ask the paper to run something.

The daily totals scrolled down the screen. The eleven days of the survey visits were the driest of the whole month. The data came from the Met Office. It was official and could not be argued with. It made the survey's timing look either sloppy or on purpose. Jonah read the record twice because it seemed too easy. The second time it was still true.

choices.label: Submit the objection with the full method.

nodes.body: Jonah walked the rows in November with the species list in his hand. He ticked the ones he could be sure of. The number he could be sure of was nine: the bare branches, the pond seen through the reeds, the moss on the old wall. The rest were asleep or gone or could not be named in the low grey light of late fall. The list felt thin and not enough. But it was honest. And honesty was the one thing he could offer that the survey had not.

choices.label: Submit it in the name of the orchard trust.

nodes.body: The coffee went cold on the table between Jonah and Halvor. Neither of them spoke of it. The cafe was quiet and the windows were steamed. Halvor asked his fair questions in his fair voice. Jonah gave answers that were careful and not quite whole. When it was over, Halvor paid for the coffee on the way out. It was a small act that was neither kind nor mean. The cold cup stayed on the table, untouched.

choices.label: Ask for the hearing to be public.

nodes.body: Ada sat in the shed with the paraffin heater ticking. She said speaking in rooms was not the hard part. The hard part came after, when people were kind to you about it. "Kindness after the fact is harder to bear than fighting it before," she said. Jonah understood she was talking about something older than the orchard, older than the notebooks. It was an old hurt that had healed but still ached in certain kinds of weather.

choices.label: Give the developer the dossier first.

nodes.body: Every page of the file was numbered. Every figure had a source. Every unknown part was stated in plain words at the bottom of the page it belonged to. The work ate up two evenings. It cut away four of the points Tobe had listed. A complaint you have already seen and answered stops being a complaint. The file was thicker now and heavier. Jonah felt its weight like a kind of sure-footed trust.

choices.label: Put the found volumes into the record.

nodes.body: The two 1917 books were in a box marked WAR COMMITTEE MISC on the lowest shelf in the basement. They were not damaged and sat right where they had been put a hundred years ago. Jonah lifted them out and opened the first one. A pressed leaf fell from the pages at July. It was crisp, brown, and kept its shape. The handwriting was the same tidy copperplate as the first book in Ada's shed. The dates went on without a break. The missing years were missing no longer.

choices.label: Ask Abara to attend in person.

nodes.body: Jonah put the two books back on the shelf in Ada's shed. He didn't tell anyone where they had been. The full record was now on all six shelves—a hundred and fourteen years with no breaks. But the story of the missing years was a story only Jonah knew. The gap was filled, and the record was stronger for it. Still, the filling had been done quietly. That quietness sat in Jonah's chest like a held breath. The notebooks were whole, and their wholeness was a secret.

Jonah did not pick a release date, so the deadline picked one. What went in was the version that happened to be done that Friday. The dossier was nearly complete, but not quite. Anyone who read it closely could see the missing pieces. The committee noted the gaps and the rushed sections. They considered the objection on its merits, which were less than they could have been. The work was done, but it wasn't done as well as possible. The gap between finished and ready was the gap between the dossier and what it might have been. Jonah thought later that knowing who Faulks was might have made the difference. It might have given the dossier a shape it lacked. But that knowledge had stayed unused on a page of his exercise book.

The objection went in with a hundred and fourteen years of data, a stated method, and a custody note from the archive. It also had nine species Jonah could swear to even in November. On top was a covering page of just eleven words. These were not the words from the gate but new ones. Jonah had written them at the kitchen table: the site is of long-term scientific interest, evidenced by the attached record. The form was signed, dated, and sent. The waiting began.

nodes.body: A name that was not a person was harder to answer unkindly. The Orchard Hill Trust took an afternoon to set up. It needed three signatures: Ada's, Mrs Cassar's, and Jonah's mother's. She signed without pause and then made tea. The trust was now a legal body, a name on a form. It could hold the data, make the objection, and receive the replies. The developer's lawyers would have to send their letters to an organisation. Not to an old woman or a twelve-year-old boy. That small shift in words mattered more than Jonah had expected.

Let Ada read her page.

nodes.body: A public hearing meant neighbours in the room and a note-taker writing it all down. It meant Faulks would have to answer out loud. In writing, a surveyor could hide behind careful words and the passive voice. But out loud, in a room of people, the answers would have to be given in real time to real questions. That was either a gain or a risk. It all depended on what Faulks said and how he said it.

choices.label: Sit in the front row and wait.

nodes.body: Handing the dossier to the developer before the hearing was either fair play or a wasted edge. Ada thought it was the first. Tobe thought it was the second. Ada said that surprising people with proof was not the same as convincing them. Tobe said that giving them time to make up answers was just what the survey had done to them. The argument was polite and still open. Jonah had to decide whose advice to follow.

choices.label: Pass the frame along the table.
Let the room go quiet.
Wait outside while they decide.

nodes.body: The two war books went back into the record. They were put in with the receipt that explained them. The gap on the shelf became the most powerful part of the whole dossier. The missing years had been found and returned. The story of their loss and recovery was itself proof of the care with which the record had been kept. The committee could see that the notebooks were not just raw facts. They were a steady act of attention. It stretched across wars, decades, and the plain passage of time. Its continuity was its own argument.

nodes.body: Dr Abara would come to the hearing. She would say only what she could defend. That was less than Jonah wanted but more than anyone else in the room would have. She would confirm that a hundred-year phenological record was rare and valuable. She would say six weeks of frost pocket data was a short but proper dataset. She would not be drawn into guessing or pushing a cause. Her being in the room would be its own statement. The committee would notice that a university scientist had taken the day to attend.

nodes.body: Mrs Cassar would bring thirty years of hive counts and a frame in a glass case. It was a perfect block of honeycomb she had kept since 2008. She kept it as an example of what healthy bees built when left alone. She wanted it noted, she said, that her early years were rough. She would not have anyone later claim she had pretended they were exact. The frame would sit on the table during the hearing. It was golden and perfect and impossible to ignore.

nodes.body: One page, chosen by Ada, read out at the hearing. It was either the cheapest trick in the room or the only true thing in it. Jonah could not decide which. The page would be read in Ada's voice. It would be a piece of the past made present. The committee would hear not an argument but a witness. Whether that witness would move them or just embarrass them was impossible to know ahead of time. That not knowing was the whole risk.

Watch the note taker write.
Pass the frame along the table.

nodes.body: The objection was accepted on its evidence, which was all Jonah had asked for. The officer's report named the series. It called it a long, unbroken local record of rare steadiness. It said the survey should be redone in May, when the site was growing. This was not a win but an opening. It was a door held ajar. The orchard would have to prove itself again in the spring. The notebooks had done their job. They had made the argument serious enough that someone had to answer it properly.

The copying was finished and lodged with the archive. Tobe checked it twice. It was open to anyone who wanted to read it. The hundred and fourteen years now lived outside the shed. They were in a digital file, a paper copy, and a custody note in Mrs Okonkwo's careful script. Whatever the hearing decided, the record was no longer fragile. It no longer depended on a single bulb, a paraffin heater, and the memory of an old woman. It had been copied and shared and made lasting. The work of a hundred years was now safe from the accidents of a single afternoon.

Jonah read the whole dossier. He saw then that the notebooks were never about the orchard. They were about people showing up, in order, for a hundred and fourteen years. Every evening, nine different hands wrote down the weather, the blossom, and the price of ladders. Nobody had asked them to. They did it because showing up was the thing they did. The data was proof, but the real proof was the chain of people. That chain was not a number. It was a choice, made again and again. They never knew what their record-keeping would one day be asked to prove.

The panel's first question was why the survey should not stand. The rainfall record answered it in about ninety seconds. Tobe had a single sheet. It showed the survey dates laid over the August rainfall data. You could see the link without any words. All four visits had taken place in a dry spell. That dry spell had hidden the very things the survey was meant to find. The panel chair nodded slowly. It was the way people nodded when an answer was both a surprise and enough.

nodes.body: Someone on the panel called the notebooks "amateur." The word hung in the air of the council room. Jonah answered with the custody note, the double-typing records, and the marked doubts. He laid each paper on the table in order. "Amateur" was not an insult when the work was done with care. And care could be proved. The member who had spoken did not say sorry. But the word was not said again. The silence that followed was the kind that meant a question had been answered.

Decide what to tell the class.

nodes.body: Six weeks of frost pocket readings was short. Jonah said so before anyone else could. He told the panel what the data did and did not show. It showed a steady temperature gap. It showed a tiny climate that shaped the lower orchard. It showed a set of data that would need a full winter to be final. His honesty seemed to catch the panel off guard. The chair wrote something down that Jonah could not read from his seat. Sharing the limits of the proof was not the same as making it weak. The panel seemed to get that.

choices.label: Decide what to say to Halvor now.
Hand the series over to the archive for good.
Hold out for the road to move.

nodes.body: Faulks laid out his method in a flat voice. It was a standard method, done right, but in the wrong two weeks. He had used the right path, the right forms, and the right sample rules. But he had done it all in August, when the ground was dry and the plants were sleeping. The orchard had shut down to wait for rain. He did not enjoy saying so, and you could hear it in his voice. The method was sound, he said. The timing was just unlucky. The gap between those two truths was where the argument turned.

Read the officer report when it lands.

nodes.body: Ada read a page from March 1947. It told of ice on the water butt and eleven days of nothing. A cold snap had caught the early blossom and blackened it on the branch. She read in her normal voice, the same one she used in the shed. The room was perfectly quiet when she stopped. The page was not an argument. It was a moment, saved in ink. The silence that followed was the kind that meant something had moved. The note-taker's pen had stopped.

Decide who keeps the notebooks now.
Decide what to tell the class.

nodes.body: Jonah gave the file to the panel, the builder, and the public on the same day. He sent it by email to every address on the council's list. The edge of surprise was gone. In its place was something else. The dossier was now out in the open. Anyone could read it. The builder could not claim later that they had been ambushed by proof they had no time to check. The move cost the edge but bought openness. And openness was its own kind of power.

Decide what to say to Halvor now.

nodes.body: The hearing ran an hour late. Jonah sat through a drainage item and a fence fight. The afternoon light crept across the council room floor. By the end of the other items, his hands were calm. His nerves had burned off during the wait. The orchard item was called. Jonah stood up, and the calm held.

nodes.body: The two charts went on the easel side by side. One showed the bloom dates. One showed the frost pocket data. They stayed there all afternoon while the other items were heard. People looked at them during the drainage talk and the fence fight. Their eyes would drift to the lines on the paper. By the time the orchard item was called, the charts had already done half their job. The panel had seen the proof before a single word was spoken.

nodes.body: The note-taker wrote down the phrase "long unbroken local series." Tobe nudged Jonah under the table. They both stared straight ahead. That was the exact phrase Dr. Abara had used in her report. Its presence in the official minutes meant the panel had taken the notebooks as proof. The note-taker's pen moved on. The phrase stayed on the page. The argument had shifted, and nobody had said a word about it.

choices.label: Read the officer report when it lands.

nodes.body: Mrs. Cassar's frame went along the table inside its glass case. Every person on the panel picked it up, even the one who stayed quiet the whole hearing. The honeycomb was gold and perfect. The wax was clear in the council room light. The panel held it like people hold something they know can break and never be replaced. The frame went back in its case, and Mrs. Cassar shut the lid. The panel had seen something that a report could not carry.

choices.label: Read the conditions attached.

nodes.body: After Ada read the page from 1947, nobody spoke for eight seconds. In a council room, that is a very long time. The silence was not awkward. It felt full, like a room after a piece of music ends. The chair did not rush to fill it. Ada shut the notebook and sat down. The hearing went on, but something had changed in the room. Jonah could feel it, though he could not name it.

nodes.body: Jonah waited in the hall with the recycling poster again. Mrs Cassar told him about a swarm in 1994, on purpose and for a long time. The story had a neighbour's chimney, a bee-keeper from three villages away, and a way of getting the bees that Mrs Cassar described with care. She was not filling the quiet but giving Jonah something to hear while the panel made up its mind. The kindness of it was so on purpose that Jonah nearly laughed.

choices.label: Decide who keeps the notebooks now.

nodes.body: Jonah answered a fair question as if it were unfair. His voice got louder and the words came out faster than he meant. After that, the chair became careful with him, the way someone handles a problem more than they listen. Careful was the worst thing a chair could turn into. The rest of the hearing went on in a tone of polite patience. The decision, when it came, was measured and fair and all against the orchard. Jonah had made it a personal fight. That was not proof. The notebooks sat on the table, unused.

Jonah answered six questions with six bits of proof. Each came from the file and was placed on the table one by one. He did not answer the seventh question in a fully honest way. He said the data did not back a firm answer and he would not pretend it did. The chair gave a nod. The note-taker wrote something. The officer's report later asked for the site to be checked again in the growing season by a new surveyor. The honest seventh answer did not make the case weaker; it made the first six answers impossible to argue with.

ending.title: Six Answers and One Honest No

nodes.body: The officer's report was forty pages long. The orchard was in eight of them. The words "of no special scientific interest" were not there at all. Instead, the report pointed to the long local records, the frost pocket data, and the list of species. It set out rules that would force the builder to check the site again before any choice could be made final. Jonah read the report at the kitchen table while Ada made tea. The eight pages felt like a door that had been shut now starting to swing open.

nodes.body: Three rules were set: a new check in May by a fresh ecologist, a frost pocket study over a full winter, and all the records handed to the archive as a term for any future go-ahead. Each rule was a job. Each job was a promise. The promises would stretch the work into a second year and more. The rules were not a win but a frame. The frame meant the orchard would have to keep showing its worth, season after season, for as long as the choice stayed unmade.

Put the rota on the shed door.

nodes.body: The spine road could be moved forty metres east, for a price, the officer's report said. The row with the big Bramley tree might live through that choice or it might not. Forty metres was a field's width, a small shift on a map but huge on the ground. The council would have to weigh the cost of the move against the worth of the trees. The Bramley stood on the hilltop, its roots in ground never built on. Its life now hung on a number in a fund and a line on a plan.

choices.label: Sit with the 1917 volumes.
Watch the May resurvey happen.
Write the hundred and fifteenth year.

nodes.body: The notebooks could go to the archive, or to the trust, or stay in the shed. Each of those three paths was a promise to someone not in the room. To Ada, who had kept them for sixty years. To Mrs Okonkwo, who had offered them a lasting home. And to the future, which would need the record to go on. The choice was not about where to put them but about keeping things going. That keeping going was what made the notebooks worth keeping in the first place.

Start the winter frost study properly.
Train somebody to read the hands.

nodes.body: Thirty people had typed the notes from the 1930s in the school hall on Thursday afternoons. They deserved a fair account of what their work had done and not done. Jonah wrote a letter to the class. He set out the hearing, the new rules, and the road that might move forty metres east. The letter was careful and full of thanks. It did not pretend the orchard was safe. The class had given their time, and that time had counted. The letter was a way to say that without pledging more than the truth could bear.

Decide how the record continues.

nodes.body: The readings meant a thing only if they went on. Going on was a choice someone had to make every single morning. The thermometers did not read themselves. The notebook did not fill itself. The list on the shed door would need names on it, week after week, month after month, for as long as the frost pocket study took. Someone had to choose to carry on. The choice was not one act but many of them, made at dawn in the cold, over and over.

Sit with the 1917 volumes.
Watch the May resurvey happen.

nodes.body: Halvor asked the same question again in the hall after the hearing. This time the true answer was not the same. The orchard was not safe, but it was not gone either. What would make Jonah stop now was not giving in. It was a process: a real survey, a fair hearing, a choice made on proof, not ease. Halvor heard him out and did not argue. The coffee cup from the shop was still on a sill somewhere, cold and lost. The question had changed because things had changed, and both of them knew that.

Let the rota lapse in December.

nodes.body: The notebooks went to the stable room at the archive with a gift deed, a public list entry, and a lasting right for Ada to read any of them when she liked. Mrs Okonkwo set them on the shelf herself, in time order. The gap where the war years had been was no longer a gap. It was now a note in the catalogue that told how they were found again. The record would outlast all who had been in the fight: the builders, the councillors, the surveyors. The hundred and fourteen years would sit in the room kept at a steady heat, with its window facing north. They would wait to turn into a hundred and fifteen, then two hundred, then more than anyone could count.

The road went forty metres east. It curved around the top of the hill instead of cutting through it, and the row with the big Bramley stood. The condition about the winter frost study was written in full into the permission. The developer would have to fund the checking for five years. The data would belong to the trust and be stored in the archive. The orchard was not a nature reserve or a protected site. But it was a place that had been noticed and recorded and argued for. That noticing was what saved it. The Bramley stood at the top of the hill in the rain, bare now in December. The road curved away from it as though the tree had always been there, waiting to be seen.

Dr Abara said the honest answer was that one October bloom proved nothing and a hundred and fourteen years of dates proved a great deal. The tree had not been a signal but a question, she said, and the question was not why it had flowered in October but why anyone had been there to notice. The answer to that question was in the notebooks, in the nine hands and the six shelves and the evenings in the shed, and the answer was not data but attention. The orchard had been watched, and the watching was the thing that had made the evidence possible, and the evidence was the thing that had changed the decision, and the decision was the thing that would keep the orchard standing long enough for the next question to be asked.

A full winter of dawn readings needed nine people. It needed a spare thermometer in case the first one broke. It needed someone to do December, the hardest month. The mornings were dark and the grass was frozen. The urge to stay in bed was stronger than any talk of data. Jonah looked at the calendar. He saw the blank squares of December. He knew the rota would hold only if someone made it hold. That someone was going to have to be him.

nodes.body: The nine different hands could be taught in an afternoon to anyone patient, Ada said. The teaching turned out to be the part she liked most. She sat with the young volunteers at the kitchen table and showed them how the letters sloped and where the ink had faded. Her voice was patient and exact. The volunteers listened with the care of people who knew they were learning something that could not be learned from a screen. The hands would outlast her. The teaching was a way of making sure they did.

nodes.body: A trust with three names and no purpose was just a form. Deciding what the trust was for took four meetings and one argument. The argument was about what it should be. Should it be a fighting body or a caring one? Fighting for the orchard or simply looking after it? That difference was the difference between a weapon and a home. The argument ended in a deal that left nobody fully happy, but everyone was pleased enough. The trust's purpose was written down, signed, and filed. The form became something real.

The record could not carry on alone, and the archive could not carry it on, and the trust could not carry it on. Only a person could carry it on, writing in a notebook in the shed. The paraffin heater ticked and the bulb swung in the draught. That person had to choose to do it, evening after evening, the way Ada had chosen for sixty years.

nodes.body: The second thermometer cost eleven pounds from the hardware shop in town. It was the most important buy anyone made that year. With two thermometers the frost pocket study could go on even if one failed. The data would not have a gap in it, and a gap was the thing that could ruin months of work. Eleven pounds. The future of the orchard rested on it as much as on any legal fight or council report.

nodes.body: The rota went up on the shed door where the chart used to be. By January, two names had been crossed out and four new ones added. People dropped out and others stepped in. The rota was a living thing. It changed with the weather, the season, and the usual demands of people's lives. The crossings-out were not failures. They were just fixes. The names that stayed were the ones that mattered.

nodes.body: The two war volumes were just like all the others. They were full of weather, ladders, wasps, and one line from September 1917 about the horse. The horse had been taken and given back. The note about it was short and dry. The rest of the volume carried on as though nothing had happened. The war had passed over the hill and left only a receipt and an empty spot on a shelf. The notebooks had simply carried on, the way they always did.

nodes.body: The May resurvey took nine days and four people. It found sixty-one species. Nobody had ever recorded one of them on this hill before. It was a small orchid growing in the shade of the old wall. The ecologist who found it knelt in the wet grass and took photos from three sides. The species list was no longer thin. It was rich. That richness was the answer to the eleven words on the gate. It was an answer written not in arguments, but in the slow, careful work of looking properly.

nodes.body: Jonah wrote up the day in a new notebook, in his own hand. He did it badly. The letters were bumpy and the dates a little crooked. Ada watched from her chair by the heater and said nothing. Her silence was not anger. It was something else. It felt like a gift of trust. The record went on being a record. It was flawed but it carried on. The hundred and fifteenth year began with a boy's handwriting in a blue notebook adding his line to the six shelves. The shelves accepted it without a word, the way they had accepted every hand before his.

The December readings stopped for eleven days over Christmas. The people on the rota were away. Those who had said they would cover forgot, got sick, or just did not show up. The gap in the data was small. It was eleven days out of a hundred and eighty, but it was a gap. No amount of care later could fill it. The winter series had a hole. The final report showed that hole as a dotted line where data should have been. That dotted line was a reminder. It showed that keeping things going was fragile, and eleven days of not paying attention could undo months of work.

The resurvey report listed sixty-one species. It gave the frost pocket its own paragraph. It said the orchard should be watched, not cleared. The word 'watched' showed up three times in the final advice. Each time was a small win. It was a sign that the site was not dead but living. Living things changed. Change needed watching. The report was not a pardon. It was a promise. And that promise would stretch on for years.

nodes.body: Four months had passed. Two friendships were strained. There was one letter Jonah should not have sent. And there was a grandmother who was more tired than she had been in October. Ada moved more slowly now. Her writing in the new notebook was shakier than before. The cost of the argument was clear in the way she sat down at the end of the day and closed her eyes. The orchard had been defended, but it had taken something from everyone. That something was not coming back.

nodes.body: Almost all of the work stood, in the same order. The one thing missing was the thing Jonah had said about Faulks. He would not say it again. The rest was all there. The copies, the charts, the data from the frost pocket. The letters to the families. The Thursday afternoons in the school hall. The dossier was solid. The record was complete. The case had been made honestly. The single moment of blame was the only piece Jonah would take back if he could. Knowing that was itself a kind of learning. And the learning was worth keeping.

nodes.body: In April the whole row blossomed at once, just the way it should. The big tree at the top was neither early nor late. The blossom was pink and white and plain, and the bees worked it in the thin spring sunlight. The orchard looked exactly the way it had looked every April for a hundred and fourteen years. The October bloom did not happen again. The notebooks wrote down the date without saying anything more, the way they wrote down everything. And the fact that things were normal was its own kind of comfort.

nodes.body: The orchard was watched. The series was public and growing. In the end, the thing that had saved it was not one October morning. It was a hundred and fourteen ordinary evenings. Evenings when someone had walked up the hill. They had opened a notebook and written down the weather, the blossom, the frost, the wasps, and the price of ladders. They had kept the record without knowing what it would one day be asked to prove. That keeping was the proof. The notebooks sat in the archive and on the shelf in the shed. They sat in the digital file on Tobe's laptop. The hundred and fifteenth year was underway. And the record went on, as it always had, because someone had decided that it should.

Jonah understood at last that a record was not proof and never had been. It was only the reason a person could be believed when they finally said something. The notebooks had not won the argument by themselves; they had made it possible for Ada to speak and be heard, for the data to be checked and confirmed, for the frost pocket to be measured and cited. The record was the foundation, and the foundation was not the building, but without it nothing else could stand. The notebooks were not evidence of anything except attention, and attention was the thing that made all the other evidence possible.

The last thing Jonah did was index the six shelves. Nobody had ever done this. He listed every volume by year and hand and subject. The index filled a notebook of its own. That notebook sat at the end of the shelf like a key to a door. The index took a year, working in the evenings after school and on weekends. By the time it was done, the orchard had been resurveyed twice. The road had been moved. The frost pocket study had become a long-term programme. The index was the most useful thing on the hill, and Jonah had made it. Making it was the last piece of the work.

The next October the Bramley did not bloom. The road ran forty metres east, where it had been moved to. The picking was normal and huge and took nine days. The apples came off the trees in baskets and crates. The shed filled with the smell of them. The notebooks wrote down the picking weights in the usual column. The October bloom of the year before was a single line in a single volume. The hundred and fifteenth year was just a year, like all the others. Its ordinariness was the very thing they had been fighting for. The orchard was still an orchard. The road went around it. The trees went on being trees, the way they always had.

The eleven words were still in the back of Jonah's exercise book. He had copied them in his own handwriting on the day the notice went up on the gate. He read them again, months later. They no longer felt like a threat. They were the reason there was now a hundred and fifteen years of anything. The reason the record had been copied, checked and sent in. The reason the road had been moved and the orchard watched. The eleven words had not been beaten but answered. The answer was six shelves of notebooks. A winter of dawn readings. A trust with three signatures. The words were still there, and they were not untrue. But they were no longer the last word. And that was enough.

The notebooks were safe in the archive. They were listed in the public system, and nobody added to them. The last entry was the one Ada had written on the evening of the October bloom. After that, the pages were blank. The series was closed. It was a whole thing from 1911 to now. In twenty years it would be a set of papers that people studied, rather than a thing that was kept. The chain was broken. Not by fire or flood, but by the simple fact that nobody had picked up the pen. The record was finished and complete. And its being complete was a kind of loss.
